title: Gradient Preconditioning for Efficient and Reliable Reward-Guided Generation
claim: Prior regularizers either leave the latent structured or need slow iterative projection; ours removes spatial correlation while staying close to the initial latent in one step.
layout: 4 columns left-to-right, latent and image pairs, cosine-similarity row beneath
description: A single-row comparison of four columns separated by double vertical rules. Each column shows a latent image beside the sampled image it produces. The first column, the initial latent, is a black-and-white noise field with a clear letter A pattern. Its sampled image is a washed-out, near-blank texture. The second column, the L_norm baseline, looks nearly identical to the initial latent and gives the same faded output. The third column, MPGR (Hwang et al., 2025), has a noisier latent with a faint A and produces a dark upright piano. The fourth column, Ours, has a latent that looks like uniform white noise with almost no visible A and produces a pink upright piano. A bottom row of cosine similarity to the initial latent reads 1.000, 0.222 and 0.548. The eye goes first to the letter A and then to the pianos.
caption: \textbf{Effectiveness of Projection onto $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbb{R}}$.} Starting from an initial latent encoding the letter ‘A’, we compare two regularization methods and our projection. Our method preserves high cosine similarity to the initial latent while reducing the spatial correlations. Unlike [ref], which requires slow gradient-based iterative projection, our method guarantees optimality with a single operation. The images are sampled from FLUX with the prompt "Piano".
abstract: We propose a gradient preconditioning method that makes reward-guided generation with one-step generative models both efficient and reliable. Test-time noise optimization can unlock substantially better reward-guided generations from pretrained generative models, but it is prone to reward hacking that degrades quality and is often too slow for practical use. We precondition reward gradients by projecting them onto a carefully designed white Gaussian noise feasible set, a compact spectral set with blockwise norm constraints that tightly captures the statistics and spatial uncorrelatedness of white Gaussian noise. This preconditioning reshapes each gradient update into a noise-aligned direction, driving faster and more effective reward ascent while preventing reward hacking. The projection is closed-form and matches the $O(N \log N)$ complexity of FFT, adding negligible overhead in practice. In experiments on FLUX with four reward models, our approach reaches a comparable Aesthetic Score using only 30% of the wall-clock time required by the state-of-the-art regularization-based method.
